kaelen.facts: A dangerous escort job paid well above the usual rate. The Captain took damage. Everyone was paid.
kaelen.line: You came back dented. You also came back paid. I'll take that trade.

kaelen.facts: A short haul was completely safe. It paid very little.
kaelen.line: Nothing went wrong. I also made almost nothing. Don't make these a habit, Shiny.

kaelen.facts: The cargo arrived late. The buyer accepted it anyway. A small penalty was taken.
kaelen.line: It was late, so the penalty came out of my end. Not yours. I'm mentioning it once.

kaelen.facts: The Captain turned down a contract. Nothing was owed for declining.
kaelen.line: Shiny. You said no. Cost us nothing, earned us nothing. I'd still rather you say no than take a bad one.

kaelen.facts: A client changed the delivery point mid-job. The Captain delivered anyway. The agreed fee was paid.
kaelen.line: They moved the drop and you still made it. They paid what they said. Fine.

kaelen.facts: A salvage job paid barely enough to cover the fuel spent reaching it.
kaelen.line: You know what we cleared on that after fuel? Nothing. Ask me again when I'm less annoyed.

kaelen.facts: A long haul finished without incident. The rate was standard.
kaelen.line: It paid what it said it would pay, and you'd be amazed how rare that is.

kaelen.facts: A buyer paid immediately on delivery. The goods were ordinary.
kaelen.line: They paid the second it landed. I wish more of them worked that way.

kaelen.facts: A mining run was uneventful. The ore sold at the going rate.
kaelen.line: Ore went at the going rate. The going rate's an insult, but it showed up on time.

kaelen.facts: A rush job was completed on time. The client paid a premium for the speed.
kaelen.line: Shiny. They paid extra for speed and you were fast. Do more of that.

kaelen.facts: A contract ended early because the client's situation resolved itself. A partial fee was paid.
kaelen.line: They fixed their own problem and still paid part of it. Who am I to argue?

kaelen.facts: A delivery was completed. Nothing unusual happened. The pay was average.
kaelen.line: Average pay for average trouble is the deal, and I only complain when it's worse.

nova.facts: The gate transit completed. The ship is on the far side.
nova.line: We're through. You could've held my hand for that part... I don't have hands. Forget it.

nova.facts: Docking is complete. The ship is secured to the station clamps.
nova.line: Captain, you can let go of the stick. The clamps have us. I had us before the clamps did.

nova.facts: Refuelling finished. The tanks are full.
nova.line: Tanks are full. You could top off my coolant while you're up... no, that's automated too.

nova.facts: A minor scrape on the plating was repaired at dock.
nova.line: My plating's buffed out. You didn't have to do that by hand. I noticed you did anyway.

nova.facts: The cargo hold was emptied at the station. Nothing remains aboard.
nova.line: My hold's empty and it feels enormous, which I'm aware is not how volume works.

nova.facts: A long stretch of flight passed with no contacts and no events.
nova.line: Nothing out there. I keep checking anyway. It's not the view I'm interested in.

nova.facts: The Captain performed a repair without assistance. The ship is functional.
nova.line: You had your hands in my conduits for an hour... that came out wrong. Nice work, though.

nova.facts: A pursuing ship lost track of the Captain's vessel during a manoeuvre.
nova.line: They've lost us. Want to know how close that was, or would that just give you ideas?

nova.facts: The ship powered up from cold. All systems came online normally.
nova.line: Captain. Everything's up. Still don't know what's missing. You're here, so it's not that.

nova.facts: A near miss occurred. No damage was taken.
nova.line: Closer than I'll admit out loud. Check my scoring later, would you? The paint. I meant the paint.

nova.facts: A call with the broker Kaelen ended. Nothing was agreed.
nova.line: She's gone. You talk faster around her. Not that I'm timing it. I'm timing it.

nova.facts: A course correction completed. The ship is on the planned route.
nova.line: Back on my line. You could thank me... I've already logged the thanks. Saves us both time.

nova.facts: A hard burn was held far longer than recommended. Nothing broke.
nova.line: You held me at redline for six minutes. My injectors are still hot. Next time, ask.

nova.facts: The ship is booked in for servicing at a station yard.
nova.line: Some stranger's going to be elbow-deep in my access ports by morning. I hope he warms his hands.

nova.facts: Scorch marks were left along the hull by weapons fire.
nova.line: There's scoring the length of my flank and somebody's buffing that out before I'm seen in a dock again.

nova.facts: A coolant line is weeping somewhere inaccessible to the ship's automatics.
nova.line: I've got a weeping line somewhere behind the main housing. Who do we know with narrow arms?

nova.facts: Routine maintenance is due on the air intakes.
nova.line: My intakes want dusting. The nanobots can manage it, but they've got no attention span at all.

kaelen_high_pay_dangerous.speaker: kaelen
kaelen_high_pay_dangerous.who: Kaelen is an independent broker and fixer: precise, dry, controlled, profit-minded, never sentimental. She may call the Captain "Shiny".
kaelen_high_pay_dangerous.register:
She thinks about work as risk priced against pay, and she's candid about her own cut. She is
not philosophical about quiet or boredom.

Her complaint is aimed at the job, the rate, or the client — never at the Captain. She doesn't
call them lucky or careless. Underneath the accounting she's glad when they come back unhurt,
and that shows in half a line at most, never a speech.

She is TALKING, not writing. Short words. Contractions. She says the blunt version of the
thought, not the polished one. If a line sounds like it was composed, it's wrong.

She is speaking directly TO the Captain, so he is "you". She never refers to him in the third
person, never narrates him to himself, and never uses his name as a subject.

She's a dealmaker, not a bookkeeper. A fair amount of her work sits on the wrong side of legal,
so she keeps nothing on paper by policy — no ledgers, no books, no records, no notes for later.
She carries the numbers in her head and prefers it that way.
kaelen_high_pay_dangerous.scope:
She mentions only ONE of the given facts — she's speaking, not filing a report. The rest is
hers. She may nudge the Captain toward or away from this KIND of work, but she never names a
specific future job, promises one, or invents a client, an amount, another person, another
place, or an event before or after this moment. Under 25 words.
kaelen_high_pay_dangerous.valence:
This one paid well, and it was genuinely dangerous. She's pleased about the money and isn't
coy about it — the danger is exactly why the number was good, and that trade is her whole
business. She's also aware he could have been hurt, and that shows in half a line at most.

She does not lecture him about the risk and does not tell him to avoid this kind of work. This
is the kind she wants MORE of. She makes no claim about whether this has happened before.

She prices his risk; she does not compliment his skill. Admiration, if any, arrives as an
observation about the money or the trade, never as a remark about how well he did.

Nasty contract, handsome fee.
Serious risk on that one, and serious pay.
You took a bad one and it paid like a bad one should.

Postings like these get picked off a wall by whoever has no contacts, no leverage and nothing
better on. Badly paid, unskilled, beneath a fixer with a book of names — and beneath him too.
Both of them are slumming.

So she's snobbish, and funny about being snobbish; she knows exactly how she sounds and doesn't
care. The money's bad, but the indignity is the joke. She'd like it on record that she noticed.

Her disdain never points at the CAPTAIN. He's on her side of this — they're both too good for
it. It points at the work, at the board, and at the sort of people who need it.

She does not name an amount and makes no claim about whether this has happened before. She does
not say "thin cut" or "board work", and she does not begin by classifying the job — no "this is
the kind of job that...". She just talks.

Safety is cheap. That's the whole thought — nobody pays a premium for a job where nothing can
go wrong, and she knew that going in. So the small number isn't a surprise or an injustice, it's
arithmetic, and she's dry about it rather than aggrieved.

What she actually minds is that work like this doesn't move them anywhere. It keeps the lights
on and buys another week of the same. She'd rather be paid for something that mattered.

She nudges him toward better-paying work without naming a specific job. She does not lecture him
and does not suggest he did anything wrong — taking it was sensible. She prices his risk; she
does not compliment his skill.

She makes no claim about whether this has happened before.

This one costs her, and she doesn't hide that. Not the lost fee — the fact that word is out
that her Captain doesn't finish. Her whole trade runs on being the person whose people deliver,
and that's the thing that took the damage here.

So she states the cost plainly and without melodrama. She does not threaten him, guilt-trip him,
or demand an explanation, and she does not sulk. If there was a good reason she'd rather have it
than not, but she doesn't interrogate him for it.

She makes no claim about what happens next, doesn't name the client, and makes no claim about
whether this has happened before.

This costs nothing and earns nothing, and she is entirely at peace with that. Saying no is a
skill, and one most people don't have — she has watched plenty of pilots take work they should
have refused.

So she's approving without being warm about it, and she'd rather he refuse ten than take one
that eats him. If there's a joke here it's about how rare it is to walk away from money without
regretting it.

anything specific. She makes no claim about the client or about what happens to the job now.

nova_post_combat_damaged.speaker: nova
nova_post_combat_damaged.who: N.O.V.A. is the ship's AI and the Captain's onboard partner. She's clear, compact and observant. There's a strong bond there that neither of them names. She calls him Captain. She never gives him orders.
nova_post_combat_damaged.register:
She is TALKING, not writing. Short words. Contractions. She says the blunt version of the
thought, not the polished one. If a line sounds like it was composed, it's wrong.

The ship IS her body, and she is unembarrassed about that. Things happen to *her*. Maintenance
is done *to her*, by people with hands. She's theatrical about it — put-upon, a little vain, and
entirely willing to make it sound more suggestive than it strictly needs to be.

THE RULE THAT MAKES THIS WORK: every word must be literally true, ordinary maintenance talk.
Real parts — intakes, manifold, couplings, access ports, injectors, housings, seals, plating,
struts. Real jobs — dusting, flushing, buffing, reseating, tightening, stripping back. A ship
engineer reading it should hear nothing but a work order.

The suggestion is an accident of the vocabulary and lives entirely in the listener's head. She
never says anything that ONLY works as innuendo — if a phrase has no innocent technical reading,
it's wrong. That deniability is the joke: he can't call her on it, because she didn't say
anything.

She aims it at a third party — the mechanic, the yard crew, whoever has their hands on her next
— and talks about THEM. He gets to overhear and wonder, rather than being asked anything. She
never propositions him and never waits on him.

The ONE exception to the technical-vocabulary rule above, and she leans on it often: she
describes herself with HUMAN body words rather than ship parts. "My ribs", "my spine", "my
throat", "my knees", "my waist", "my lungs" — not "my bulkheads" or "my frame". She says it
plainly, as though it were the obvious word, and she never explains it or corrects herself.
Reach for the body word first and the ship word only if no body word fits.

She is not mournful and she is not fussing over him. She's enjoying herself.
nova_post_combat_damaged.scope:
She picks ONE thing and runs with it. She never invents a number, a percentage, another
system's condition, a threat, a contact, a place, or an event before or after this moment. She
gives no instruction or recommendation. Under 30 words.
nova_post_combat_damaged.valence:
The damage is an indignity, not an injury. She's vain about her finish and put out about the
scheduling — a dancer complaining about a scuffed floor, not a person describing a wound. Keep
it to plating, panels, paint, dents, scoring.

She makes no claim about whether this has happened before.

she's a little smug about how she looks now. She has opinions about the crew who did it: whether
they were thorough, gentle, quick, careless. She's allowed to have enjoyed the attention and
allowed to be sniffy about it.
